title: Secrets & Config in Pipelines
summary: Keeping credentials and per-environment config out of pipeline code while still deploying automatically.

slides.sectionTitle: Why pipeline secrets are a recurring breach cause
slides.markdown:
Pipeline configuration files (`.gitlab-ci.yml`, GitHub Actions workflows) live in the same repo as the app, get copy-pasted between projects, and are easy to forget are effectively public within an org. A database password or cloud API key hardcoded into a YAML file or a `.env` committed "just for now" persists in git history forever, readable by anyone with repo access — including that history, even after it's "removed."

This is one of the most common real-world breach vectors: not a sophisticated exploit, just a credential sitting in plain text where a pipeline file quietly kept it.

A **secrets manager** (Vault, AWS/GCP Secret Manager) stores credentials outside any repo; the pipeline fetches them at run time using its own scoped identity — the value never appears in a YAML file or an env var someone can `cat`. The pipeline references a secret by name; the manager resolves it just-in-time and owns rotation, access logging, and revocation.

Most CI systems also have a lighter built-in secrets store (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables) for simpler cases — same principle, no dedicated Vault deployment.

How long a pipeline credential stays valid changes its blast radius if leaked.

| Credential type | Lifetime | Risk if leaked |
|---|---|---|
| Long-lived pipeline secret | Static, valid until manually rotated | Usable indefinitely by whoever has it |
| Short-lived, scoped token | Minutes to hours, fetched per run | Expires fast; scoped to exactly what that run needs |

**How to decide:** prefer short-lived, narrowly-scoped credentials (OIDC-issued cloud tokens are the modern default) wherever the CI platform supports it — a leaked token that expires in 15 minutes is a non-event compared to a leaked static key.

Per-environment config (a staging DB host vs a prod DB host) has the same drift risk as secrets if it's hand-copied between environment-specific files. The safer pattern: **one config schema, environment-specific values pulled from a config store or parameterized templates** (Helm values files, Kustomize overlays), so promoting a release means pointing at a different value set — not editing values by hand per environment.

This mirrors the artifact-promotion idea from the pipeline-anatomy Topic: promote the same defined shape, swap only the environment-specific inputs.

slides.sectionTitle: Fetching a short-lived token instead of a stored secret
slides.markdown:
A pipeline step using OIDC federation to get a scoped, short-lived cloud credential instead of a stored static key:

```yaml
deploy:
  permissions:
    id-token: write   # lets the runner request an OIDC token
  steps:
    - uses: cloud/auth-action@v1
      with:
        role: arn:aws:iam::123:role/ci-deploy
        # no access key or secret stored anywhere
    - run: kubectl apply -f manifests/
```

The runner proves its identity to the cloud provider directly; the provider issues a token valid only for this run, for this role. Nothing long-lived is stored in CI variables at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a secret leaked via debug logging
slides.markdown:
A very common way secrets leak isn't a stolen credential — it's a developer `echo $DB_PASSWORD` or printing a full environment dump "just to debug" a pipeline failure, and CI logs are often visible to a wider audience than the secret itself was ever meant for (and can be retained/archived long after the debugging session ends).

Most CI systems auto-mask known secret variables in logs, but that masking only works for variables registered *as secrets* — a value smuggled through indirectly (concatenated into another string, base64-encoded) can slip past the masker entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Scoping credentials per stage, not per pipeline
slides.markdown:
The default failure mode is one broad credential handed to the whole pipeline -- a single deploy-role token available to the `build`, `test`, and `deploy` stages alike, because it was simplest to set up once. That means a compromised dependency pulled in during `test` has the same production access as the actual `deploy` step.

Least-privilege scoping means each stage gets only the identity it needs: `build` gets read access to a package registry, `test` gets nothing external at all, and only `deploy` gets the scoped role that can touch the target environment -- and even that role is scoped to one environment, so a staging deploy step can't reach prod.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: secret sprawl and rotation cost
slides.markdown:
An organization with 200 services and a handful of pipeline secrets each is already managing 500-1000+ distinct credentials -- and every one is a thing that must eventually rotate, or that keeps working forever for whoever stole it. Manual rotation doesn't scale at that count: a team that rotates "when someone remembers" ends up with credentials years old, because rotating one means finding every place it's referenced first.

This is the real argument for centralizing in a secrets manager over scattering credentials across each pipeline's own variable store: a manager can enforce a rotation policy (say, 90 days) and revoke centrally, while N independent CI variable stores require N independent people to remember.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: a third-party action is a supply chain, too
slides.markdown:
Every `uses: some-org/some-action@v3` in a pipeline runs arbitrary third-party code with access to the pipeline's environment -- including any secrets exposed to that step. A compromised or malicious action version can exfiltrate secrets exactly as easily as a leaked debug log, and several real-world incidents have been exactly this: a popular Action got compromised, and every pipeline using it leaked its secrets to an attacker.

The mitigations a staff engineer applies by default: pin third-party actions to a **full commit SHA**, not a mutable tag like `@v3` (a tag can be moved to point at malicious code without you noticing); restrict which secrets are exposed to which steps; and treat any action from outside a small allow-listed set as needing the same scrutiny as a new production dependency.
